events/deutsche-messe-1526/summary: After his Latin Formula Missae (1523), Luther publishes the Deutsche Messe, a vernacular order with congregational hymns, a sermon and the words of institution sung as gospel, first used in Wittenberg in October 1525. He insists it must not become a new law.
events/schleitheim-confession-1527/summa: Swiss Brethren meeting at Schleitheim under Michael Sattler agreed on seven articles: believers' baptism, the ban, the Lord's Supper as memorial of the baptised, separation from the world, pastors, nonresistance (refusal of the sword) and refusal of oaths. Sattler was executed months later.
events/schleitheim-confession-1527/cause: Need for unity among scattered Anabaptists
events/schleitheim-confession-1527/conse: Separatist nonresistant ethic of Mennonites and Amish
events/riksdag-of-vasteras-1527/summary: King Gustav Vasa's diet at Västerås transferred church property and jurisdiction to the crown and permitted evangelical preaching, beginning the Swedish Reformation. The Lutheran character of the Church of Sweden was confirmed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, which adopted the Augsburg Confession.
events/riksdag-of-vasteras-1527/causes/0: Royal need for revenue after independence from the Kalmar Union
events/riksdag-of-vasteras-1527/causes/1: Evangelical preaching of Olaus and Laurentius Petri
events/riksdag-of-vasteras-1527/conseque: Church of Sweden under royal authority
events/marburg-colloquy-1529/summary: Philip of Hesse brought Luther and Zwingli together to unite the Protestant cause. They agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles but not on Christ's presence in the Lord's Supper: Luther insisted on 'This is my body', Zwingli on a spiritual and memorial understanding.
events/marburg-colloquy-1529/causes/0: Political need for a Protestant alliance
events/marburg-colloquy-1529/consequence: Lasting division between Lutheran and Reformed Protestants
events/augsburg-confession-1530/summary: Drafted by Philip Melanchthon and presented to Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg on 25 June 1530, the confession set out Lutheran doctrine — justification by faith, the church as where the gospel is purely preached and sacraments rightly administered — and the abuses corrected. It remains the chief Lutheran confession.
events/augsburg-confession-1530/causes/0: Imperial demand for a statement of faith
events/our-lady-of-guadalupe-1531/title: Apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe (tradition)
events/our-lady-of-guadalupe-1531/summar: According to the Nican Mopohua (published 1649), the Virgin Mary appeared to the Nahua convert Juan Diego at Tepeyac in December 1531, leaving her image on his cloak. Documentary evidence before the 1640s is scant and historians debate the tradition's origins, but Guadalupe became the central symbol of Mexican and Latin American Catholicism.
events/our-lady-of-guadalupe-1531/causes: Encounter of Indigenous and Spanish religion after conquest
events/our-lady-of-guadalupe-1531/conseq: Symbol of Indigenous and mestizo dignity
events/act-of-supremacy-1534/summary: Parliament declared Henry VIII 'the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England', breaking with Rome after the pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Thomas More and John Fisher were executed for refusing the oath; monasteries were dissolved from 1536.
events/act-of-supremacy-1534/consequence: Church of England independent of Rome
events/munster-rebellion-1534/summary: Apocalyptic Melchiorite Anabaptists led by Jan Matthys and Jan van Leiden took over Münster, proclaimed it the New Jerusalem, introduced community of goods and later polygamy. Besieged by Catholic and Lutheran forces, the city fell in June 1535 with mass executions.
events/munster-rebellion-1534/consequenc: Menno Simons' turn to a peaceful Anabaptism
events/calvin-institutes-1536/summary: John Calvin published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion in Basel and was persuaded by Farel to stay in Geneva. Expelled in 1538 and returning in 1541, he organised the city's church with consistory, academy (1559) and missionary outreach to France.
events/calvin-institutes-1536/consequenc: Reformed theology and polity spread across Europe
events/danish-church-ordinance-1537/summ: After his victory in the civil war (the Count's Feud), Christian III arrested the Catholic bishops (1536) and introduced a Lutheran Church Ordinance (1537), drafted with Johannes Bugenhagen, for Denmark and Norway; it was formally applied in Norway in 1539.
events/danish-church-ordinance-1537/cons: Lutheran state churches of Denmark, Norway and Iceland
Superintendents (later bishops) appointed by the crown
events/jesuits-founded-1540/summary: Paul III approved the Society of Jesus founded by Ignatius of Loyola and companions including Francis Xavier. Bound by obedience to the pope for missions, the Jesuits became the spearhead of Catholic renewal, education and global mission.
events/jesuits-founded-1540/consequences: Missions in Asia, the Americas and Africa
events/council-of-trent-1545/summary: Meeting in three periods, Trent answered the Protestant challenge by affirming Scripture and tradition, the deuterocanonical books, justification as a process involving cooperation with grace, seven sacraments, transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass. It also reformed clergy, mandated seminaries and required bishops to reside in their dioceses.
events/council-of-trent-1545/longText: Trent was the Catholic Church's definitive response to the Reformation and shaped Catholicism until the Second Vatican Council. Its decree on justification (1547) taught that justification is God's free gift, received through faith, which truly renews the believer, and that one may grow in it and lose it through mortal sin; it condemned the view that justifying faith is merely confidence in mercy. The council defined the canon including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and Maccabees, and declared the Vulgate authentic for public use. Disciplinary decrees attacked absenteeism, pluralism and ignorance among clergy. Protestants were invited to the second period but found the conditions unacceptable. The Roman Catechism (1566), revised Missal (1570) and breviary followed. Protestants saw Trent as entrenching errors; Catholics see it as clarifying doctrine and launching a genuine reform. The 1999 Joint Declaration states that the mutual condemnations of the 16th century do not apply to the Lutheran and Catholic teaching as presented there.
events/book-of-common-prayer-1549/summar: Under Edward VI, Thomas Cranmer’s English prayer book replaces the Latin rites (first used Whitsunday, 9 June 1549), provoking the Western Rising. Revised in a more Reformed direction in 1552, restored under Elizabeth (1559) and revised again in 1662, it became the liturgical bond of the Anglican Communion.
events/jesuit-mission-to-japan-1549/titl: Francis Xavier begins the mission to Japan
events/jesuit-mission-to-japan-1549/summ: Francis Xavier, with the Japanese convert Anjirō, landed at Kagoshima on 15 August 1549 and preached in several cities. Jesuits adapted to Japanese culture; by 1600 there were perhaps 300,000 Christians, including daimyō, before persecution under Hideyoshi and the Tokugawa.
events/jesuit-mission-to-japan-1549/caus: Xavier's meeting with Anjirō in Malacca
events/valladolid-debate-1550/title: Valladolid debate on the rights of Indigenous peoples
events/valladolid-debate-1550/summary: Before a royal junta, Bartolomé de las Casas argued that Indigenous Americans were rational peoples with rights who must be evangelised peacefully, against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda's Aristotelian case that they were 'natural slaves' who could be conquered. No formal verdict was issued, but the debate is a landmark in the history of human rights.
events/valladolid-debate-1550/consequenc: Theological roots of universal human rights
events/chaldean-union-1553/title: Yohannan Sulaqa consecrated in Rome: origin of the Chaldean Catholic Church
events/chaldean-union-1553/summary: In 1552 opponents of hereditary patriarchal succession in the Church of the East elected Yohannan Sulaqa, abbot of Rabban Hormizd monastery, who travelled to Rome and was consecrated patriarch by Pope Julius III in 1553. Sulaqa was killed in 1555; after a complex history of shifting lines, a single Catholic 'Patriarchate of Babylon of the Chaldeans' was consolidated in 1830 under Yohannan Hormizd.
events/chaldean-union-1553/causes/0: Hereditary succession within one patriarchal family
events/chaldean-union-1553/causes/1: Catholic missionary contacts and Ottoman–Safavid politics
events/chaldean-union-1553/consequences/: Rival patriarchal lines (Eliya and Shimun) for three centuries
Chaldean Catholic Church formally consolidated in 1830
Patriarchal seat moved to Baghdad in 1950
events/peace-of-augsburg-1555/summary: The Holy Roman Empire recognised Lutheranism alongside Catholicism, allowing each prince to determine his territory's religion — later summarised as cuius regio, eius religio. Reformed and Anabaptist believers were excluded.
events/peace-of-augsburg-1555/causes/0: Failure to defeat the Schmalkaldic League permanently
events/peace-of-augsburg-1555/consequenc: Tensions leading to the Thirty Years' War
events/first-national-synod-paris-1559/t: First national synod of the French Reformed churches
events/first-national-synod-paris-1559/s: Delegates of French Reformed congregations met secretly in Paris in May 1559 and adopted a confession of faith (the Gallican Confession, revised at La Rochelle in 1571) and a discipline establishing consistories and synods.
events/first-national-synod-paris-1559/c: Rapid growth of Reformed churches under Genevan influence
events/scottish-reformation-1560/summary: In August 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction, forbade the Mass and approved the Scots Confession drafted by John Knox and five colleagues. The First Book of Discipline (1560) and later Andrew Melville's Second Book of Discipline (1578) shaped a Presbyterian church order.
events/scottish-reformation-1560/causes/: Lords of the Congregation's rebellion against Mary of Guise
English intervention and the Treaty of Edinburgh (1560)
events/scottish-reformation-1560/consequ: A century of conflict between Presbyterian and episcopal church government
events/synod-of-debrecen-1567/summary: A synod at Debrecen under Péter Méliusz Juhász adopted the Second Helvetic Confession, marking the consolidation of a Reformed church among Hungarian speakers; the Heidelberg Catechism also became a standard. Debrecen came to be called 'the Calvinist Rome'.
events/synod-of-debrecen-1567/causes/0: Spread of Swiss Reformed theology in Ottoman-divided Hungary and Transylvania
events/synod-of-debrecen-1567/consequenc: Reformed colleges at Debrecen and Sárospatak
events/roman-missal-1570/title: Roman Missal of Pius V (Quo primum)
events/roman-missal-1570/summary: Implementing the Council of Trent, Pius V promulgates a revised Roman Missal by the bull Quo primum (14 July 1570), requiring its use throughout the Latin Church except for rites at least two centuries old (e.g. Ambrosian, Mozarabic, some religious orders). It remained essentially unchanged until 1962.
events/roman-missal-1570/consequences/0: Liturgical uniformity of Latin Catholicism for four centuries
